learn.title: Talking about the future: will, be going to, present continuous and simple present
learn.html:
In English there isn't just one «future»: the form depends on why you are talking about the future.

FormWhen it is usedExample
will + verbyou decide something at the moment you speak; predictions based on what you knowI'll get it! Our project won't be finished on time.
be going to + verbplans already decided; predictions with evidenceWe're going to have dinner together. My boss is going to make us work late.
present continuousfixed, specific plans (they sound more definite)I'm meeting Anna after my class.
simple presentschedules and timetablesThe class starts at 7:00 tomorrow.
  • For information about the future (facts), you can use will or be going to: You'll be back on Friday? / You're going to be out of town.
  • For personal plans that are already decided, don't use will: say I'm going to call her or I'm calling her at five.
  • Negative form: won't (will not), isn't going to.

watch.wrong: A: I need a pen. B: I'm going to get you one right now.
watch.right: I'll get you one right now.

watch.wrong: The meeting is starting at 9:00 every Monday.
watch.right: The meeting starts at 9:00 every Monday.

watch.wrong: I will visit my grandparents on Sunday. We bought the tickets already.
watch.right: I'm visiting my grandparents on Sunday. We already bought the tickets.
watch.why: Plan already decided and organized: present continuous or be going to.

watch.wrong: I'm going to to call you later.
watch.right: I'm going to call you later.
watch.why: Be going to + base verb, without another to.

learn.title: What's advisable: had better, ought to, might want to
learn.html:
To give advice or say what is advisable, use these expressions followed by the base form of the verb (without to, except ought to).

ExpressionStrengthExample
had better ('d better)strong; there are consequences if you don't do itYou'd better do something quickly.
ought tomedium; advice or a good ideaI ought to do some volunteer work.
might want tosoft; a friendly suggestionYou might want to take a colleague with you.
  • Negative of had better: You'd better not be late.
  • Don't use had better for general advice (about everyone): for that, use ought to or should. People ought to exercise more.
  • Had better looks like a past form because of had, but it refers to the present or future. It is contracted to 'd.

watch.wrong: You had better to call your boss.
watch.right: You had better call your boss.
watch.why: Had better + base verb, without to.

watch.wrong: I ought go to the gym more often.
watch.right: I ought to go to the gym more often.

watch.wrong: Everybody had better exercise every day.
watch.right: Everybody ought to exercise every day.
watch.why: Had better isn't used for general advice.

learn.title: What's necessary and what you prefer: have got to, going to have to, don't have to, would rather
learn.html:
These structures are also followed by the base form of the verb.

IdeaStructureExample
necessary (strong)have got to ('ve got to)I've got to decide by next week.
necessary (in the future)be going to have toI'm going to have to do something about it.
not necessarydon't / doesn't have toYou don't have to spend time on this.
preferencewould rather ('d rather)I'd rather stay in my current job.
negative preferencewould rather notI'd rather not change jobs.
  • Have got to is stronger than going to have to.
  • Don't have to does NOT mean «you must not»: it means «it isn't necessary». To prohibit, use mustn't or can't.
  • With would rather there is no to: I'd rather stay, not I'd rather to stay. To compare: I'd rather stay home than go out.

watch.wrong: She doesn't has to wake up early.
watch.right: She doesn't have to wake up early.
watch.why: After doesn't comes the base form: have.

watch.wrong: I'd rather to stay at home.
watch.why: Would rather + base verb, without to.

watch.wrong: I've got finish this report today.
watch.right: I've got to finish this report today.

watch.wrong: You don't have to smoke here. It's forbidden.
watch.right: You can't smoke here. It's forbidden.
watch.why: Don't have to = not necessary; the prohibition is can't / mustn't.

learn.title: Connecting ideas: as long as, provided that, unless
learn.html:
These expressions join two conditional ideas. They are mainly used in writing.

ExpressionMeaningExample
as long asif, only ifYou can go out as long as you finish your work.
provided thatif, only if (more formal)I'll help you provided that you tell me the truth.
unlessunless; if ... notUnless you find time, there is no point in having the recordings.
  • Unless = if ... not: Unless you study, you'll fail = If you don't study, you'll fail.
  • After unless the verb is affirmative (it already contains the «no»): unless it rains, not unless it doesn't rain.
  • With future time, the verb in the clause with as long as / unless is in the present: unless you finish, not unless you will finish.

watch.wrong: I won't go unless it doesn't rain.
watch.right: I won't go unless it rains.
watch.why: Unless already means «if not»; the verb is affirmative.

watch.wrong: You can borrow my car as long you drive carefully.
watch.right: You can borrow my car as long as you drive carefully.
watch.why: The full expression is as long as.

watch.wrong: I'll call you unless I will have time.
watch.right: I'll call you unless I have time.
watch.why: After unless / as long as, use the present, not will.

learn.title: Ending a call and saying goodbye
learn.html:
To try to end a call:

  • I'd better go. / I've got to get going. / I've really got to go.
  • I'm going to have to run.
  • Can I call you back? / I'll call you later.

Informal goodbyes (the words in parentheses are usually left out):

  • (I'll) Talk to you later. / (I'll) Catch you later. / (I'll) See you later.
  • (I've) Got to go. / (I'd) Better go.
  • (It was) Nice talking to you.

Example: A: Is this a good time to talk? B: Not really. Can I call you back?

Use will for a decision, be going to and the present continuous for plans, the simple present for a timetable, two things you have got to do (have got to / going to have to), one thing you don't have to do (don't have to) and a condition with as long as or unless.

A have got to or going to have to

write.model:
Next week is going to be very busy. On Monday, I'm meeting my boss at nine o'clock because we have a long meeting about a new project. The meeting starts at nine and finishes at eleven. I've got to prepare a report before that, so I'm going to start tonight. On Tuesday, I'm going to visit my grandmother, and I'm having lunch with my cousin on Wednesday.

I forgot to buy a gift for my sister's birthday, so I'll go to the mall tomorrow and buy her a book. I think she will like it. On Thursday, I'm going to have to go to the dentist because my tooth hurts. I don't have to work on Friday because it's a holiday, so I'm going to sleep late.

The bus to the beach leaves at seven on Saturday morning, and I'll go with my friends as long as the weather is good. Unless it rains, we are going to stay all day. I'd rather relax on the sand than go to a party, so I'll bring a book.

write.prompt: Write 120 to 160 words: an email to a colleague about a work problem (too many tasks or a deadline). Give them three pieces of advice (had better, ought to, might want to), say what you would rather do (would rather) and use two expressions with do or make.
targets: had better / ought to / might want to

Two expressions with do or make (make a list, do research)
An unless or as long as
write.model:
Hi Sara,

I know you have too many tasks this week, and the deadline for the report is on Friday. I want to help you, so here is some advice. First, you'd better make a list of everything you have to do. Then you ought to start with the most important work. You might want to ask our manager for one more day, because the report is very long.

I'd rather not work this weekend, but I will help you if it is necessary. Unless we finish the data by Thursday, we will have a problem. As long as you send me the numbers tomorrow, I can do some research for the last part. I also think we should make a plan together and make an appointment with the boss to talk about the deadline.

Please don't worry. We can do this! Let me know what you think.

Best,
Pablo

reading.title: Less is more at work
reading.intro: Read the text about Marcela and answer.
paragraphs: Marcela is a project manager at a software company in Monterrey. Last year she had too many things to do: three projects, five meetings a day and about two hundred emails every morning. She tried to do everything at the same time. She answered emails during meetings, wrote reports on the phone and ate lunch at her desk. She was always tired, and she made a lot of mistakes.

One Friday, a colleague told her, "You'd better stop multitasking. You're going to get sick." Marcela didn't want to listen at first, but she read some research about it. The research said that people who multitask make progress more slowly and get distracted more easily. She decided to do something about the problem.

First, she made a list of her priorities. She also set a rule: she answers emails only twice a day, at 10:00 and at 4:00. She learned to say no, too. "I'm not going to take on any new jobs unless I have enough time," she told her boss. She had to make some difficult decisions, but she made up her mind quickly.

Now her day is different. In the morning she works on the most important task, and she doesn't check her phone. Her team can interrupt her as long as it is urgent. She goes to fewer meetings, and she usually leaves the office at six. Next week she's going to start a volunteer program with her colleagues. They're meeting on Saturday morning to plan it.

Marcela says her stress level is much lower now. "I meet my deadlines, I make fewer mistakes, and I sleep better," she says. "You ought to try it. You don't have to change everything in one day, but you'd better start soon. Unless you set priorities, your work will drive you crazy."
